html:
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was the joint state of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, from 1569 to 1795, one of the largest countries in Europe. The map shows it in 1650, 1700 and 1715; the chart's state bar for it is Poland-Lithuania.

The Union of Lublin of 1569 turned a union of rulers into one state with one parliament, the Sejm. Its nobles, a large share of the population, elected the king and held wide rights they called the Golden Liberty. The Warsaw Confederation of 1573 promised peace between religions, rare in Europe then. Grain shipped down the Vistula through Gdańsk made the nobles rich.

The 1600s brought disaster. The Khmelnytsky Uprising of Ukrainian Cossacks in 1648 and the Swedish invasion called the Deluge in the 1650s devastated the country. King John III Sobieski still led the relief of Vienna in 1683. But the liberum veto, by which one deputy could block the Sejm, left the state weak, and its neighbours took it apart in the partitions of 1772 to 1795.
